newsitem.title: USA: Green groups question Clinton's Utah monument act.
newsitem.headline: Green groups question Clinton's Utah monument act.

text.p: First mining supporters accused the White House of playing politics. On Friday, environmental groups started to think the same.

It's all over President Clinton's sweeping gesture last year, staged at the Grand Canyon at the height of the presidential campaign, to create the nation's newest national monument, Grand Staircase-Escalante, in southern Utah.
Counties around the monument counting on mining jobs were so mad they recently sued the administration for setting aside the 1.7 million acres of spectacular canyon land.
While Clinton's move was meant to prevent a big coal mine from spoiling the scenery, it did not stop DuPont Co. subsidiary Conoco from drilling for oil on state property on the land.

On Friday, protesting a quarter of a mile away from Conoco's drill site in the Utah monument -- and with a toppled 20-foot wooden oil rig next to the Washington Monument near the White House -- environmental groups sent a message to the president.
"Oil rigs in national monuments. Hell, no, Conoco," the Southern Utah Wilderness Coalition's banner said.

With drilling equipment clanging in the background, Larry Young, co-chairman of the coalition, said in a telephone call from Grand Staircase-Escalante that Clinton's grand action last year now seemed empty.

"Today, when listening to this noise and industrial development in our nationl monument, I wonder whether Clinton was engaged in a presidential act or a political act," Young said. "It begins to feel like it was more of a political act."
Conoco is now waiting for permits from the U.S. Bureau of Land Management to drill five wells on leases it has on the federal portion of the land.
The Interior Department agency was set to issue the first permit at the end of this month, but was flooded with comments on its environmental assessment, which it is revising.

The bureau's fluid minerals director in Utah, Robert Hendrix, said a final decision on the permit was now expected in late August. Only after that, will the agency start reviewing applications for the other permits, which could require a new environmental study.
When he created the monument, Clinton said valid existing leases would be honoured. But the administration also said it would write a land management plan, which is not yet complete.
"To approve the drilling permit really mocks the planning process," said Cindy Shogun, spokeswoman for the southern Utah wilderness groups.

She said the government should suspend the leases -- a move the company requested in the hope that it could arrange a land swap. But Shogun said the Interior Department was holding out for a better option, "Interior's thinking (Conoco's) going to come up dry and go away."
Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt alluded to that Thursday answering questions at the National Press Club, saying, "It's best to sit back and analyse the results (from the state lease drilling)."
